In a recent development, to test this, we scored each architecture type for enrichment of known cell state signatures. Using published gene sets for classical LGR5-positive crypt base columnar SCs (CBCs) and LGR5-negative regenerative/fetal-like SC populations8,14,32,33,34, we found that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for regenerative/fetal-like programmes, whereas classical CBC signatures were enriched in glandular architectures (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). EMT is a further hallmark of malignant progression, co-opted from developmental and wound-healing programmes to facilitate tumour cell dissemination35. Moderately and highly fragmented architectures were strongly enriched for published EMT signatures (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5i). Thus, glandular and solid architectures associate with the classical CBC state, while fragmented architectures associate with fetal/regenerative SC programmes and EMT.

Sources indicate that to determine whether the transcriptional signatures correspond to distinct cellular phenotypes, and to validate the relationship between cell states and architecture at scale, we applied multiplex immunofluorescence to the initial TMA cohort. MSS patient samples were stained with a panel of antibodies targeting CBC, fetal/regenerative SC, EMT and proliferative states (Methods). Single cells were segmented and clustered based on combined marker expression36 and closely related phenotypic clusters were consolidated into seven major phenotypes (Extended Data Fig. 6a). These comprised differentiated tumour cell states with varying expression levels of CDX2 and PROX1, a transcriptional repressor induced in the fetal/regenerative state that suppresses non-intestinal lineage genes to enable phenotypic plasticity8. We also detected a highly proliferative population that retained CDX2 expression. Moreover, annexin-A1 (ANXA1)-positive cells and vimentin (VIM)-positive tumour cells formed two distinct populations. ANXA1-positive cells demonstrated increased levels of tenascin-C (TNC), a hallmark ECM protein defining the EMT programme (Extended Data Figs. 6a–c and 7a). This indicated that EMT-related features might manifest as partially overlapping programmes across phenotypic subsets rather than within a single discrete state.

Recent findings suggest that we next examined the distribution of these phenotypes across tumour architectures and confirmed that fragmented regions were enriched in regenerative and VIM-positive EMT-like populations, whereas other architectures were preferentially associated with differentiated tumour cell states (Fig. 2i). Notably, fragmented architecture was not exclusively composed of regenerative or EMT-like populations, but also included areas dominated by well-differentiated or proliferative tumour cell states, indicative of state heterogeneity. Conversely, glandular architecture was not exclusively composed of differentiated cells, but also contained clusters of regenerative tumour cells (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

This partial overlap prompted us to examine whether specific architecture–cell-state combinations carried distinct prognostic information. Stratifying patients by tumour cell phenotype composition revealed that the combination of fragmented architecture and regenerative phenotype was associated with the worst survival, most prominently in the tumour core (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 7b,c), whereas cell phenotype composition alone was not predictive of outcome in CT (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Patients with fragmented regenerative tumour cores predominantly also displayed this signature at the IM, whereas the reverse was less frequent (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the state originating at the IM and propagating towards the tumour core. Collectively, combining architectural and phenotypic information provides a prognostic signature superior to either modality alone.

The tight association between cell states and tissue architecture raised the possibility that tumour architectures, like cell states, undergo dynamic transitions during cancer progression. Given that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for both EMT and regenerative SC states, we first examined whether these programmes co-exist within the same cells or define distinct populations. To assess the potential existence of hybrid EMT/regenerative states and their subsequent diversification, we mined two CRC single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets12,37. Subclustering of MSS patient tumour epithelial cells and GSEA analysis for CBC, EMT and regenerative SC signatures revealed that EMT and regenerative signatures were enriched within the same Leiden clusters in both datasets, while CBC signatures occupied separate clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Examination of individual cells both within specific clusters and across the full dataset identified a substantial population with high co-enrichment of EMT and regenerative signatures, indicative of a hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Co-expression of key marker genes including VIM, SNAI1 (encoding SNAIL1), ANXA1 and EMP1 in single cells further supported the existence of this hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8g). CBC signatures were not correlated with regenerative SC signatures, suggesting that cells must exit the CBC state before acquiring hybrid identity (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f).

Sources indicate that diffusion pseudotime analysis of a subclustered dataset encompassing CBC, regenerative and EMT states (clusters 0, 3, 4 and 6), initiated from the most stem-like cluster identified by CytoTRACE scoring38, revealed a trajectory from CBC towards a hybrid EMT/regenerative population. This trajectory was characterized by progressive downregulation of CBC and stemness-associated transcription factors ASCL2 and HMGA1 and the identity marker LGR5, followed by upregulation of regenerative SC markers and plasticity-associated KLF family transcription factors and, ultimately, upregulation of EMT transcription factors including SMAD3 and other established EMT markers39,40,41 (Extended Data Fig. 8h–j).

In a recent development, to spatially resolve the distribution of regenerative and EMT states within tumour tissue, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell resolution multiplex immunofluorescence across whole-tumour sections, using ANXA1 as a regenerative state marker and VIM, SNAIL1 and E-cadherin/pan-cadherin ratio as EMT markers. ANXA1-positive cells were highly enriched in fragmented regions (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a), consistent with the transcriptomic data. At the tumour–stroma boundary of moderately fragmented regions, ANXA1-positive cells also exhibited EMT features, confirming co-existence of regenerative and EMT programmes at this interface (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). However, within fragmented regions, cells with high VIM expression were spatially segregated from ANXA1high cells, forming largely non-overlapping, spatially proximal populations (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 9d). SNAIL1 showed comparable expression across both populations (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 9a,c), consistent with a transcriptional continuum rather than binary state switching. The predominantly mutually exclusive but spatially proximal distribution of ANXA1high and VIMhigh cells suggests plasticity between regenerative SC and EMT states.

We next used trajectory analyses of the spatial transcriptomes to infer the most probable routes of architecture transitions during CRC progression. Glandular architectures indicated highest probability of transitioning to moderately fragmented, while solid architectures preferentially transitioned to highly fragmented (Fig. 3e). To control for potential confounding by unequal architecture representation across patients, we performed pseudotime analysis within individual patients with heterogeneous architecture distributions, using a central glandular region as the reference point and grouping regions by nearest neighbour to account for spatial proximity effects. Architecture and spatial cluster distributions within each pseudotime window were consistent near both start and end points across all three patients analysed (Fig. 3f–h and Extended Data Fig. 9e), and key CBC, regenerative and EMT marker genes showed monotonic changes along the pseudotime trajectory (Fig. 3i), indicating that architecture transitions are accompanied by corresponding changes in cell state. These transitions were recapitulated in the U-Net tile embedding space combined with multiplex immunofluorescence-based cell state classification, in which the strongest connections were found between glandular and solid architectures, and between solid and fragmented architectures, whereby transition of glandular to solid architectures corresponded to a transition from differentiated and PROX1high states to regenerative and EMT states (Extended Data Fig. 9f).

Together, these analyses demonstrate that cell states and tissue architectures co-evolve within individual patients, and that EMT and regenerative programmes form a continuum, distinct from the CBC state, which can diversify towards regenerative SC or EMT-dominant identities.

To investigate the mechanism driving architecture-linked cell state diversification, we first examined whether the distinct nuclear morphologies observed across architectures in whole-tumour resections reflected the same co-evolutionary relationship seen in the TMAs. Single-cell segmentation and quantitative nuclear morphology analyses confirmed that glandular architectures associated with nuclear elongation while fragmented architectures associated with increased circularity (Extended Data Fig. 10a), consistent with the TMA findings. We next examined microenvironmental signals potentially driving this transition. Spatial transcriptomic scoring of the tumour compartment revealed elevated TGFβ pathway activity and higher YAP transcriptional programme scores in fragmented architectures (Fig. 4a,b), and immunofluorescence confirmed increased nuclear YAP levels in these regions (Fig. 4c). Analysis of paired stromal compartments showed that fragmented regions were additionally enriched for T cell, natural killer cell and myeloid cell transcriptional signatures (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Collagen architecture in fragmented regions was characterized by increased structural complexity and reduced fibre coherence, and TNC showed similar, albeit less pronounced, architectural variation (Fig. 4d). Thus, fragmented architectures show coordinated stromal and ECM remodelling and elevated tumour cell TGFβ and YAP activity, consistent with an altered mechanical microenvironment.

Sources indicate that to examine causative relationships between changes in the ECM mechanical microenvironment, YAP and cell states, we turned to disease modelling using patient-derived organoids that were whole-genome sequenced and validated to contain APC and TP53 mutations. A shallow scRNA-seq analysis showed that, like the in vivo tumours, the organoids also displayed hybrid EMT/regenerative SC states and mutually exclusive classic CBC and regenerative SC states (Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). We then examined whether changes in architecture could promote transition from a classic CBC to hybrid or diversified cell states. To this end we selected two independent patient-derived CRC organoid lines that, based on the scRNA-seq data, had high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4 CBCs and only low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR regenerative SCs (lines 1 and 2; Extended Data Fig. 11a,c). We plated these two lines onto engineered colonic sheets42, where cells could grow unrestricted on flat surfaces or be confined in finger-like protruding channels (Fig. 4e–g). Analysis of RNA levels using in situ hybridization showed heterogeneous cell phenotypes with regions enriched for ANXA1high cells that were distinct from LGR5high cells (Fig. 4e). Notably, ANXA1high cells were enriched at bottoms of the confined finger-like channels whereas LGR5high cells showed no preferential localization (Fig. 4e). EMT states as marked by VIM expression were homogeneously low and distributed within the channels with partial overlap with ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4e).

Industry observers note that notably, while both patient lines responded to the architectures, the response of line 2 was stronger than line 1 (Fig. 4e,f). Examination of differences between these lines in the scRNA-seq data revealed that, while both lines when grown in Matrigel contained high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4-positive SCs and low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive regenerative SCs, line 2 revealed a more prominent signature of β-catenin activity (Extended Data Fig. 11d), which is central to the regulation of stemness and EMT in the colon43,44. This was associated with high expression of the β-catenin target gene and plasticity transcription factor SOX48,40 (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). Consistent with its elevated β-catenin transcriptional signature, high nuclear β-catenin was seen only in line 2 cells (Fig. 4f,g). Moreover, while YAP1 expression was not substantially different between the lines, line 2 showed higher baseline activity, as indicated by an enriched YAP transcriptional signature (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). However, within this line, nuclear β-catenin was seen only in the unrestricted, flat areas of the engineered sheets, while it was undetectable in the channels enriched in ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4f,g). This implied that, while intrinsically high β-catenin activity correlated with the responsiveness to tissue architecture, potentially through promoting SOX4 expression, confinement of cells into channels suppressed WNT activity and promoted the emergence of an ANXA1-positive cell state. The role of β-catenin activity in tuning the responsiveness to mechanosignalling was confirmed by culturing the responsive line 2 in the presence or absence of Chir-99021 to activate canonical WNT. Upregulation of AXIN2 and the key CBC marker ASCL2 expression, as well as elevated SOX4 and β-catenin levels in the nucleus in response to β-catenin stabilization by Chir-99021 confirmed that these cells indeed were responsive to WNT manipulation despite their APC mutation (Extended Data Fig. 11e–h), consistent with previous studies45,46. Importantly, pretreatment with Chir-99021 enhanced the impact of YAP activation on ANXA1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 11i), indicating that high β-catenin/SOX4 state enhances mechanoresponsiveness.

Recent findings suggest that to test whether mechanical compression was sufficient to promote SC fate transitions through YAP activation, we cultured the patient organoids in Matrigel, in which ANXA1 levels were initially low, and then subjected the organoids to mechanical compression47 (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 11c). Indeed, confining the organoids was sufficient to trigger emergence of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive cells with corresponding suppression of LGR5/OLFM4-positive cells (Fig. 4h). Importantly, confinement also activated YAP (Fig. 4i). However, confinement was not sufficient to promote a diversified EMT state (Extended Data Fig. 11j,k). Collectively, these data suggest that architecture-derived mechanical signals deplete the CBC state and induce a regenerative SC state but are insufficient to promote EMT, and that high nuclear β-catenin and SOX4 expression enhances the efficiency of CBC-to-regenerative SC transition.

According to recent reports, having earlier established that SMAD3 expression is correlated with progression towards EMT, while YAP activation is associated with mechanically driven regenerative SC states, we investigated whether the TGFβ1 and YAP pathways cooperate to drive cell-state diversification. Patient organoids (line 2) were treated with a LATS kinase inhibitor (TDI-011536)48 to activate YAP, recombinant TGFβ1 or both for 4 days, and then analysed using scRNA-seq. YAP activation triggered robust transcriptional state changes, whereas TGFβ1 alone had more-limited effects (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 12a). Benchmarking cell states against a previously published dataset37, which is enriched in regenerative state cells, demonstrated that YAP activation depleted the CBC state (Fig. 5c,d), consistent with observations from the mechanical compression experiments and with CBC depletion in regenerative state cells in vivo49. YAP activation also shifted the hybrid state towards the regenerative pole of the regenerative SC-to-EMT continuum (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 12b). TGFβ1 alone modestly expanded the hybrid state and moderately induced EMT transcription factor expression, while combined treatment drove more robust diversification of the hybrid state into two distinct populations (Fig. 5a–d and Extended Data Fig. 12a,b).

Immunofluorescence analysis of ANXA1 and SNAIL1 confirmed the state distinctions: TGFβ1 alone induced SNAIL1 expression, whereas YAP activation increased ANXA1, but these states remained overlapping under single-treatment conditions. Only combined treatment produced spatially separated ANXA1high and SNAIL1high populations as quantified by signal anticorrelation (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 12c), recapitulating the in vivo patient distribution (Fig. 3c,d). YAP activation also triggered nuclear shape changes and loss of heterochromatin (Extended Data Fig. 12d–f). Consistently, reanalysis of the patient tumour spatial transcriptomic data confirmed that fragmented architectures showed reduced enrichment of heterochromatin regulators (Extended Data Fig. 12g,h). This was validated at the protein level by H3K9me2,3 immunostaining of patient samples (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j). Loss of heterochromatin was associated with increased nuclear circularity (Extended Data Fig. 12k), providing a mechanistic link between YAP signalling, nuclear shape and tissue architecture.

To determine whether these cell-state transitions were coupled to behavioural consequences, we analysed organoid dynamics. Untreated organoids displayed spheroid morphology with expansive low-level growth. TGFβ1 induced cohesive invasion without substantially enhancing overall net invasion, while YAP activation triggered dispersive invasion. Combined treatment further increased the prevalence of dispersive invasion (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Video 1).

It has been revealed that to assess the in vivo relevance of these behavioural changes, patient-derived organoids (line 2) treated with LATS inhibitor, TGFβ1 or both were orthotopically transplanted into the mouse colon by endoscopy50 (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12l). Untreated organoids did not generate visible tumours, whereas all three treatment conditions did so with variable efficiency. Mice receiving combined YAP activation and TGFβ1 treatment generated tumours (Fig. 5h,i) and, as expected, YAP activation enhanced nuclear YAP in the transplanted tumours while TGFβ1 treatment enhanced SMAD2/3 activation (Extended Data Fig. 12m). Quantitative analysis revealed that the combination treatment produced the largest tumours and the only tumours that invaded the stroma (Fig. 5i). Consistently, ANXA1 expression was elevated in YAP-activated transplants but was highest in combination-treated tumours (Extended Data Fig. 12n), collectively demonstrating that cell state diversification drives tumour aggressiveness in vivo.

It has been revealed that together, these experiments demonstrate that tissue architecture and stromal signals collaborate to drive cell-state diversification and invasive behaviour. Architectural confinement suppresses β-catenin signalling to promote regenerative SC identity, while soluble stromal signals enhance EMT features. The combination of mechanical, compositional and signalling inputs from the microenvironment drives diversification into distinct SC and EMT states and potentiates tumour invasion.

Identifying the mechanisms that drive intratumoural heterogeneity is central to improving diagnostic precision and treatment outcomes in CRC. We demonstrate that tumour architecture and associated nuclear morphology are strong independent prognostic indicators, and that these features co-evolve with cell states within individual tumours. Fragmented architectures specifically associate with transition from LGR5-marked adult SCs to a fetal-like/regenerative state linked to aggressive behaviour and poor prognosis8.

The prognostic power of architecture derives from its co-evolution with plastic, aggressive cell states. Chemotherapy, wounding, inflammation and mechanical damage are known to reactivate fetal and regenerative SC programmes in CRC34,51,52,53,54,55. TGFβ1 drives WNT independence and fetal-like lineage conversion in CRC organoids56, and fibrotic stromal stiffening promotes aggression across solid tumours57. Our data implicate compressive forces from stiffened ECM in distorting tissue geometry, inducing fragmentation and promoting adult-to-regenerative SC transition. The regenerative state emerges as a hybrid with EMT features that TGFβ1 and stromal signals further diversify into spatially proximal but transcriptionally distinct SC and EMT states, suggesting a continuum in which the balance of signals determines which state predominates. Coupling of this diversification to invasion explains the association between fragmented architecture and poor prognosis, supporting a model in which disrupted tissue organization and inflammatory signalling initiate a feedforward loop driving disease aggression.

Our image analysis framework, combining nuclear and epithelial membrane immunostaining with machine-learning-based classification, offers an efficient stratification strategy independent of mutational status, and suggests that quantitative architectural analysis could serve as a tractable proxy for tumour heterogeneity in clinical decision-making.

The study uses a previously described cohort58 comprising 1,342 patients who underwent resection for colorectal cancer at Central Finland Central Hospital between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2015 and had adequate tumour samples available. Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour samples were obtained from the pathology archives of the Central Finland Central Hospital Nova, which covers all colorectal cancers diagnosed in Central Finland (the population of the area averaged around 270,000 during the study period). Associated clinical data were collected from clinical patient records by study physicians. Moreover, all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), mismatch repair (MMR) status, BRAF V600E mutation status and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of Central Finland (Dnro 13U/2011, 1/2016, 8/2020 and 2/2023) andthe Finnish Medicines Agency (Fimea, FIMEA/2023/001573). The need to obtain informed consent from the study patients was waived (Dnro FIMEA/2023/001573).

The validation dataset was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee at Helsinki University Hospital (HUS/1223/2021). Permission to use archive samples without informed consent was granted by the Finnish National Supervisory Authority of Health and Welfare (permit number Valvira Dnro 1004/06.01.03.01/2012) and the FIMEA Finnish Medicines Agency (permit number FIMEA Dnro 2021/006901). Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm cores were made in TMA Grand Master (3D Histech). For spatial transcriptomics selected full tumour samples from the same cohort were used. The authors affirm that the study was conducted following the rules of the Declaration of Helsinki of 1975, revised in 2013.

Collagen analyses were performed on a previously described cohort59 comprising an independent cohort of 1,011 patients who underwent resection for stage I–IV CRC at Oulu University Hospital between 2006 and 2020. The analysis was based on TMAs that included four 1.2-mm-diameter cores, two from the IM and two from the CT. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of North Ostrobothnia (37/2020). The patients gave written informed consent for the study. Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm IM and CT cores were made in TMA Grand Master (TMA Master II). For this cohort all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), MMR status, BRAF V600E mutation status, tumour budding based on the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC) criteria30, and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. CD3+ and CD8+ T cell densities were quantified separately in the CT and IM, converted into percentile values, averaged across the four resulting measures and categorized as low (0–25), intermediate (>25–70) or high (>70–100), following the main principles of the Immunoscore assay.

In a recent development, immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI. Imaging was performed using the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner, with each round of staining recorded as an independent image. The CZI image file contained up to five fluorescent channels. For the full tumour samples, the staining was carried out on the same slides as spatial transcriptomics, after the spatial transcriptomics analyses. To select ROIs for sample collection for transcriptome analysis, the slides were stained with Syto13, pan-CK (AF532), CD45 (AF594) and αSMA (AF647)A to visualize nuclei, epithelial cells, immune cells and stroma, respectively. Imaging of the staining was performed on the DSP instrument using 50, 200, 200, 200 ms on the FITC, CY3, Texas Red and CY5 channels, respectively. After quenching the signal, the slides were restained for the indicated markers and the signal was imaged on the DSP instrument. The single-channel images were loaded to HALO v.3.6 image analysis software for visualization, registered based on the nuclear signal and fused to generate a composite image with 8 markers (including the nuclei).

Multiplexed fluorescence immunohistochemical staining and imaging was performed in 4–6 cycles as previously described60 for two sets of antibodies, listed below, and the nuclear marker DAPI. After the first-round staining and whole-slide imaging, the fluorescence signal was bleached, the antibodies from the first-round staining were denatured and subsequent staining rounds were performed. Imaging was performed on the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner with each round of staining saved as a separate .CZI image file.

Recent findings suggest that the following primary antibodies were used: αSMA (Dako, M0851; 1:500, 1 h at room temperature), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14; 1:500, 1.5 h at room temperature), E-cadherin (BD Biosciences, 610182; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), CDX2 (Cell Signaling, 23083; 1:1,000, 1 h at room temperature), H3K9me2/3 (Cell Signaling, 5327; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Abcam, ab7753; 1:150, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Invitrogen, MA5-13156; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), PROX1 (Cell Signaling, 45546; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), Ki-67 (Dako, M7240; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), tenascin C (R&D Systems, MAB2138; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), vimentin (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-6260; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-101199; 1:50, overnight at 4 °C) and a collagen-binding peptide (generated by the laboratory of V. Weaver61; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C). For pan-epithelial (pan-EPI) cocktail staining, the antibodies (Abcam, ab7753; Invitrogen, MA5-13156; and BD Biosciences, 610182) were combined, each at 1:200, and applied for 2 h at room temperature.

Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI.

Preprocessing and segmentation were performed essentially as described previously36. In brief, TMA cores were de-arrayed using built-in tools from QuPath (v.0.5.1)62. Cores exhibiting folding artifacts, blurriness or limited tumour content were excluded from analysis. After preprocessing, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI signal using custom-trained Cellpose 2.0 models (v.2.0 and v.2.2.2)63, separately optimized for the TMA and whole-slide image datasets. The tumour and stromal compartments were identified using a multi-label U-Net trained on 30 representative cores. Pixel-level annotations were generated manually in ilastik (v.1.4.0)64 based on pan-EPI staining.

Tumour architectural subtypes were classified through a transfer-learning pipeline comprising four stages:.

Stage 1, tiling: each TMA core image was subdivided into non-overlapping 448 × 448 px (208 × 208 µm) tiles covering the full tissue area.

Stage 2, feature embedding: a multi-label U-Net was trained to segment architectural subtypes. Ground-truth masks were derived from the tumour–stroma segmentations described above, with tumour regions manually re-annotated according to three architectural subtypes: glandular (organized, lumen-forming structures), fragmented (disrupted tumour clusters) and solid (dense). Two additional classes (stroma and edge/background) were included to handle non-tumour regions. The training set comprised 196 cores selected as unambiguous archetypes of each architectural subtype. The validity of this selection was assessed by computing silhouette scores on a panel of interpretable morphological features (Fig. 1f) and comparing the archetype score to a null distribution generated from 1,000 size-matched random draws of cohort cores assigned matching per-class labels (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Each tile was then passed through the trained U-Net, and the activations at the deepest convolutional layer (bottleneck) were aggregated through global average pooling to yield a compact feature vector per tile, encoding the dominant morphological pattern without requiring a separate hand-crafted feature design.

Stage 3, tile-level classification: a multinomial logistic regression classifier (L-BFGS solver, scikit-learn) was trained on the bottleneck embeddings to assign each tile to one of five classes: glandular, fragmented, solid, stroma or edge/background. Features were standardized before classification. The training set comprised 1,154 manually annotated tiles (365 glandular, 251 fragmented, 148 solid, 199 stroma and 191 edge/background), randomly sampled from 760 cores across the cohort. Performance was evaluated using stratified fivefold cross-validation. At inference, the classifier output five class probabilities per tile; tiles dominated by edge or stroma (probability ≥ 0.5) were excluded, and the remaining glandular, fragmented and solid probabilities were renormalized to sum to one before assigning each tile to its most probable architectural subtype (argmax).

In a recent development, stage 4, patient-level classification: tile-level predictions were aggregated per sample. The proportion of tumour-classified tiles belonging to each architectural subtype was computed separately for the CT (centre of the tumour) and IM. If a single subtype accounted for more than 50% of tiles, the sample was classified as that dominant architecture; otherwise, it was labelled mixed. The trained U-Net can be reused to extract morphological embeddings from other colorectal cancer datasets, provided that a membrane staining is available and that tissue tiles are of comparable physical size to those used in this study (448 × 448 pixels, corresponding to approximately 208 × 208 µm at the imaging resolution used here); tiles acquired at a different pixel resolution can be resampled (downsampled or upsampled) to match the model’s input size. However, the tile-level logistic regression classifier generally requires retraining to account for dataset-specific differences such as staining variability, imaging conditions or cohort composition. This is the strategy that we followed when applying the pipeline to the validation and multiplex datasets in this study: the U-Net embeddings were extracted directly, while the classifier was retrained on a new set of annotated tiles for each dataset. For the validation dataset, the classifier was retrained by supplementing the original training set with 205 additional annotated tiles (44 glandular, 49 fragmented, 28 solid, 50 stroma and 34 edge/background). For the multiplex dataset, 1,886 tiles were independently annotated (740 glandular, 446 fragmented, 123 solid, 491 stroma and 86 edge/background) and used to train a separate classifier. The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193).

It has been revealed that branch lengths were quantified from the binary tumour mask by first removing small objects (<20 px) and filling small holes (<100 px area), then skeletonizing the mask using skimage.morphology.skeletonize. Small spurious branches with an arc length of shorter than 5 pixels were removed by pruning using the skan library. Branch lengths were measured as geodesic arc lengths along the skeleton paths (√2-weighted pixel distances) using skan.summarize()[‘branch-distance’].

According to recent reports, the global contour roughness of the tumour boundary was assessed by extracting all contours from the binary tumour mask at level 0.5 using skimage.measure.find_contours. Contours with fewer than five points were discarded. The remaining contours were smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 1) to reduce pixel noise. Pointwise curvature κ for a smoothed contour (x(s), y(s)) was computed by finite differences:.

where primes denote derivatives with respect to the contour parameter. Absolute curvature values were summed over all contours and normalized by the total number of contour points N to yield mean roughness per unit length.

Lumens within the binary tumour mask were detected by filling all holes (scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes) and subtracting the original mask. The resulting lumen mask was labelled, and each lumen area (in pixels) was measured through skimage.measure.regionprops.

For each cell centroid, the Euclidean distances to its k = 3 nearest neighbours were computed using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors with a BallTree algorithm. For each cell, the mean, s.d., coefficient of variation and maximum of the k neighbour distances were stored as features.

The local nuclear orientation order (Ψk) was computed for each cell using its k = 3 nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, the orientation angle θ was obtained by projecting the cell’s orientation vector (defined by its longest axis) onto a fixed reference direction. The nematic order parameter was then calculated as:.

yielding a value between 0 (random orientations) and 1 (perfectly aligned neighbours).

Stroma proximity was determined by computing, for each tumour cell centroid, the minimum Euclidean distance to the set of stroma cell centroids using pairwise distance computation (scipy.spatial.distance.cdist).

Tumour–stroma ratio was calculated by measuring the total pixel areas of the tumour and stroma compartments from the segmentation mask and computing the ratio of tumour pixel count to stroma pixel count.

Recent findings suggest that the fragmentation index was computed by first constructing a spatial proximity graph of all tumour cell centroids, where an edge connects any two cells of which the Euclidean distance is within 80 pixels (radius-based connectivity using a BallTree). Louvain community detection was then applied to this unweighted graph to partition cells into spatially coherent communities. The fragmentation index was calculated as the number of detected communities divided by the cell count.

Industry observers note that whole-core fluorescence images were segmented into 12 tissue compartments with a multi-scale tumour/stroma classifier, and tumour islands were defined as connected components of the tumour class on the cleaned compartment map after upsampling to image resolution. The stromal compartment was restricted to a strict definition that excluded muscle, vessel, adipose, dense-stroma and debris classes. For each tumour island, a peri-tumoural region of interest was constructed as the 50 µm band immediately outside the island border, intersected with the strict stroma mask. Within this region, fibre body masks were obtained for the collagen I and TNC channels (analysed independently) using a fine-tuned U-Net applied at a probability threshold of 0.5.

From each body mask, we derived three independent descriptors of the underlying fibre network65: (1) the box-counting fractal dimension of the binarized mask, capturing network roughness and branching complexity; (2) the mean structure-tensor coherence within the mask, ranging from 0 for isotropic networks to 1 for perfectly aligned fibres; and (3) the median local fibre thickness, computed as twice the Euclidean distance transform sampled along the fibre skeleton and converted to micrometres using a pixel size of 0.325 µm. Features were emitted per (image × island × channel × distance band × stroma definition × architecture) so that all downstream summaries remained traceable to the underlying islands and fluorescence pixels. To avoid within-image pseudoreplication, every subsequent comparison was performed on per-(image × architecture) means, obtained by averaging each feature across the islands sharing the same architecture within an image.

Industry observers note that whole-slide image immunostainings were registered using the warpy workflow in ImageJ and QuPath. Whole-slide images were subsequently divided into non-overlapping tiles of 1,000 × 1,000 pixels and selected for downstream analysis in a manner analogous to TMAs, including tumour/stroma classification and nuclear segmentation. For each nucleus, the average nuclear intensity of markers (ANXA1, SNAIL1) was quantified. For cytoplasmic markers (E-cadherin, ANXA1, VIM), the nuclear contour was dilated by 5 pixels to approximate the cytoplasmic region, from which the average cytoplasmic intensity was computed. Single-cell profiles were then clustered using the Leiden algorithm at a resolution of 0.1.

Sources indicate that for each whole-slide-image tile, we computed a spatial-coherence score that quantifies whether cells with the same label group together or segregate. First, for every cell we counted its 12 immediate closest neighbours that shared the same label and averaged this count across all cells in the tile. Next, we generated a null range by randomly shuffling the position of all cells 100 times, repeating the same neighbour counting for each shuffle; the average value from these shuffled sets was taken as the expected mean. The score was then calculated as (observed – expected_mean)/(expected_max – expected_mean). A score above zero means cells with the same label cluster together more than would be expected by chance (attraction), a value of zero corresponds to a random arrangement and a negative value denotes spatial repulsion, where same-label cells are less likely to be adjacent than expected by chance.

TMA cores were identified using the dearrayer functionality in QuPath. Background illumination correction and background subtraction were subsequently performed for each core and staining round using PyBaSiC. TMAs were registered across six staining rounds using the DAPI channel as a reference. All cores underwent semi-manual quality control to remove samples that were damaged, exhibited poor registration or contained absent/very low tumour content.

Nuclear segmentation was performed using the Cellpose cyto3 model with the DAPI channel as the input. Tissue pixels were classified into tumour, stroma, tissue fold, autofluorescence, necrosis and background using an iterative supervised approach in ilastik until good visual agreement between pan-EPI signal and tumour masks was achieved across cores. For each cell, mean marker intensities were extracted using pyradiomics, and nuclear shape features were computed using a custom Python pipeline. To approximate cytoplasmic signal, nuclear masks were expanded by three pixels using expand_labels from skimage. We also computed, for each nucleus, the mean value of the ilastik pixel-classification probability map to derive cell-level classification confidence metrics.

Before clustering, cells with extreme nuclear areas were removed by excluding the lowest 1st percentile and highest 99th percentile. Tumour cells were then selected based on a tumour probability threshold of >0.5 and processed using a standard Scanpy workflow. Data were scaled using scanpy.pp.scale with max_value = 10, such that values were truncated to a maximum of 10 after scaling. Principal component analysis was performed using the maximum available number of components, and a k-nearest-neighbour graph was constructed with n_neighbors = 50. Clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm with the igraph-based implementation.

Recent findings suggest that for patient-level grouping, normalized phenotype distributions were used as input for hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage). The number of patient groups was determined based on biological interpretability and stability of the resulting clusters.

Tile-level U-Net embeddings were z-scored and used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph, visualized by t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) was computed on the three architecture classes (glandular, fragmented, solid, assigned by argmax of the renormalized U-Net probabilities after removing edge and stroma tiles) and overlaid on the t-SNE. Diffusion pseudotime was computed from a diffusion map of the same embeddings, rooted at the most confident glandular tile, and tiles were grouped into 40 equal-width pseudotime bins. Within each bin, architecture probabilities were averaged, and cell phenotype fractions (cells assigned to tiles by centroid position) were averaged and renormalized to unit sum.

Spatial transcriptomics was performed using the GeoMX-DSP platform (Nanostring/Bruker). Eight patients with stage II/III CRC were selected from the TMA cohort based on presence of architecturally heterogeneous tumours. Samples were prepared according to recommendations from the vendor for FFPE slides, including baking for 60 min at 60 °C, dewaxing and antigen retrieval with ER2 for 20 min at 100 °C, fixation in NBF (10%), incubation in NBF stop and proteinase K treatment (15 min at 37 °C). These steps were performed on the Leica BondRX autostainer. The slides were incubated with the probes overnight and, after stringent washes, were stained with Syto13, pan-cytokeratin (AF532), αSMA (custom conjugated on AF647) and CD45 (AF594) antibodies to detect tumour and stromal microenvironments. ROIs (67, 61, 96 and 59 for the four slides, carrying patients 1 and 2, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, and 7 and 8, respectively) were segmented for pan-cytokeratin positivity to collect 82, 94, 141 and 63 areas of interest (AOIs) representing tumour and tumour–stroma boundary. Each ROI yielded a tumour AOI and, where collected, a stroma AOI. Transcriptomic analyses of the tumour compartment (Figs. 2f, 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 10a) used the 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. After scanning, tissue sections were additionally stained with antibodies against SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977), E-cadherin (BD, 610182), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486) and VIM (Santa Cruz, sc-6260) and imaged using Phenoimager (Akoya Biosciences).

Recent findings suggest that quality control of the sequencing data was performed in R using GeoMx packages, following standard GeoMx QC guidelines. Segment filtering employed the following thresholds: minimum reads per segment (AOI) = 1,000, minimum percentage of reads trimmed = 80, minimum percentage of reads stitched = 80, minimum percentage of reads aligned = 75, minimum sequencing saturation = 50, minimum negative control counts = 1, maximum counts in the NTC (no-template control) well = 9,000.

In a recent development, segments with low signal were removed based on the limit of quantification. Gene filtering was applied by both compartment (tumour/stroma) and architecture type to preserve key genes in underrepresented regions. A 10% segment cut-off was used. Data were normalized using the third quartile (Q3) method.

For differential gene expression, raw counts were analysed using the PyDESeq2 Python package, with patient sample included as a covariate to control for interpatient variability. For each gene, a Wald test was used to assess differential expression; multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR. Genes with an adjusted P value (q value) below 0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed.

It has been revealed that gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the prerank function from the GSEApy Python package with 1,000 permutations. Before analysis, all genes were ranked according to their effect sizes (log-transformed fold changes) derived from the differential expression analysis. The following gene sets from previous studies were included. EMT gene sets: Wound response GO GP66, mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes)67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72. SC gene sets: crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52. High-relapse gene sets: epithelial-specific high-risk gene set, core high-relapse cells73.

Recent findings suggest that trajectory analysis was performed using PAGA74 with the sc.tl.paga function built into Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. To prepare the data, we first selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated and selected 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. PCs were batch-corrected using Harmony (v.0.0.9)76 to correct for patient-specific gene expression profiles. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs and PAGA was run on tumour architecture types.

We calculated diffusion pseudotime (DPT77) using the sc.tl.diffmap and sc.tl.dpt functions from Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. In preparation, for a patient sample, we selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs. DPT was run using a cell in the glandular region of the tumour as a ‘root cell’, representing its most unperturbed region.

The use of human CRC organoid cultures was approved as part of the iCAN Precision Medicine Flagship study reviewed by the HUS Ethical Committee and is executed based on a HUS research permit (4.5.2023 §38 (HUS/223/2023)), a Findata data permit (THL/1338/14.02.00/2022) and material transfer agreements with Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The underlying PANORG study collecting the samples to the iCAN Flagship was approved by the ethical committee of the Helsinki and Uusimaa hospital district and study site institutional review boards (PANORG ethical approval HUS/390/2021, HUS approval HUS/69/2022). The study participants provided written, informed consent for the protocols. Organoids were maintained in a mixture of 60% LWRN medium (originally established in ref. 78) and 40% human basal medium supplemented with rhEGF (R&D, 236-EG, 100 ng ml−1); LWRN was replaced with Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for no-WNT conditions. Organoids were subjected to single-cell sequencing and selected to harbour APC and TP53 mutations for the studies here.

Sources indicate that patient-derived CRC organoids were cultured in Matrigel or collagen (drug treatment experiment), after which single-cell suspensions were generated by incubation with cell recovery solution (30 min at 4 °C; Corning) followed by digestion with TrypLE Express Enzyme (5 min at 37 °C; Invitrogen). After washing with ice-cold DMEM, single cells were counted using Luna-II automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems) and loaded on a microwell cartridge of the BD Rhapsody Express system (BD) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Single-cell whole-transcriptome analysis libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions using the BD Rhapsody WTA Reagent kit (BD, 633802) and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 500 system using the High Output Kit v2.5 (150 cycles, Illumina) for 2 × 75 bp paired-end reads with 8 bp single index aiming sequencing depth of >20,000 reads per cell for each sample.

Industry observers note that UMI, complex barcode, and sample tags were extracted from raw reads and demultiplexed using a custom script (rhapsody-demultiplex; https://github.com/Bioinformatics-Service-MPI-Munster/scrna-tools). Reads were mapped using STAR (v.2.7.10a)79 (--soloType CB_UMI_Complex --soloCellFilter None --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --soloFeatures GeneFull_Ex50pAS --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA --soloCBmatchWLtype 1MM --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS2_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS3_v2_draft.txt --runRNGseed 1 --soloMultiMappers EM --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMattributes NH HI AS nM NM MD jM jI MC ch CB UB GX GN). Raw counts were imported as AnnData (v.0.10.7)80 objects in Python (v.3.9.11). We removed low-complexity barcodes using the knee plot method (1,500–3,000 counts per cell) and further filtered out cells with a high mitochondrial mRNA percentage (>50%). Doublets were predicted with scrublet (v.0.2.3)81. Finally, each sample’s gene expression matrix was normalized using scran (v.1.26.2)82, with Leiden clustering83 input at resolution 0.5.

At this stage, the samples were merged with scanpy (v.1.10.1)75. For 2D embedding, expression values were cell cycle regressed using sc.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle with G2M and S-phase gene lists from ref. 84 and sc.pp.regress_out. The expression matrix was subset to the 3,000 most highly variable genes (sc.pp.highly_variable_genes, flavor=“seurat”). We calculated and selected the top 100 PCs (sc.tl.pca), which served as basis for k-nearest neighbour calculation (sc.pp.neighbors, n_neighbors = 30). Nearest neighbours were then used as an input for UMAP layout (sc.tl.umap, min_dist = 0.3). Leiden clusters were calculated using sc.tl.leiden at resolution 0.7. Pseudotime and gene set enrichment analyses were performed as described for the spatial transcriptomics datasets. For reanalysis of the published tumour in vivo data, we chose a cell in the most stem-like cluster according to CytoTRACE analysis.

For generation of consensus gene sets, EMT gene sets (mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72) and SC gene sets (crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52) were merged and overlapping genes within and across gene sets were removed to generate the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets.

It has been revealed that all cells in the dataset were scored for the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets using the Scanpy sc.tl.score_genes function. The scores were then converted to a per-dataset rank rescaled to [0, 1]. Cells were then ordered across the CBC to RegSC–EMT axis as a composite_trajectory = (RegSC_rank01 + EMT_rank01 − CBC_rank01 + 1)/3. Cells with composite_trajectory in the top 30% of the per-dataset distribution were classified hybrid.

Recent findings suggest that for distribution across the EMT–RegSC axis, two curated marker panels were scored per hybrid cell with sc.tl.score_genes (random_state = 0): a RegSC-pole panel (GPRC5A, TSPAN1, PDZK1IP1, ANXA1, ANXA3, S100A6, S100A11, LCN2, SAA1, SAA2, KRT16, KRT17, SPP1, CD44, EMP1 and TACSTD2) and an EMT pole panel (SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST1, TWIST2, VIM, FN1, S100A4, ACTA2, MMP14, PLAU, PLAUR, SERPINE1, TIMP1). Each panel score was z-scored within its dataset, and the pole axis was defined as axis_pole = z(score_EMT_pole) − z(score_RegSC_pole). The pole-axis shift among hybrid cells was computed as Cliff’s δ = 2 × U/(n_c × n_Unt) − 1, where U is the Mann–Whitney U statistic of axis pole over the two hybrid groups. δ ∈ [−1, +1]; δ < 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the regenerative pole relative to untreated-hybrid cells, δ > 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the EMT pole. By default, untreated sits at δ = 0.

Hydrogel scaffolds were engineered as described previously42,85. A PDMS stamp (see below) with a crypt-mimicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir of the chip. To generate the ECM for the chip, bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50mL, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) at a 75/25 (v/v) ratio. After gel injection through gel-loading port, hydrogel was polymerized at 37 °C, 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as incubator) for 15 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium.

Stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS by replica moulding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion. Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consists of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 50 to 120 µm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 µm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a ×10/0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mould with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma-activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum, and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma-activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mould for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

Organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended at 40 million cells per ml in Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10 µM Y27632 after which 5 µl of cell suspension was plated onto each chip. Cells were allowed to settle for 1 h in a cell culture incubator, after which the chips were filled with Y27632-supplemented medium. The next day, Y27632 was removed and cells were cultured for 5 days. Chips were fixed in 4% PFA for 16 h at 4 °C, placed into 3D-printed custom histomoulds, filled with HistoGel (Thermo Fisher Scientific), embedded in paraffin and sectioned as described previously86. The samples were then processed for RNA in situ hybridization or immunofluorescence as described below.

Sources indicate that in situ hybridization was performed using RNAscope technology (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 30 min at 37 °C, rinsed with PBS, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and air dried. The slides were then rehydrated and 2 drops of hydrogen peroxide were added to each slide for 10 min. Primary antibodies were added and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The slides were washed and fixed with 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. After PBS washes, three drops of 1:15 diluted Protease Plus were added to slides and incubated for 10 min, followed by PBS washes.

Sources indicate that RNA probes were prewarmed for 10 min at 40 °C, cooled down and added onto slides. The slides were incubated with probes for 2 h at 40 °C, washed twice with wash buffer, subjected to stepwise hybridization with amplifier solutions for 15 min each at 40 °C, followed by application of blocker solutions. Finally, samples were incubated with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in co-detection antibody diluent for 30 min at room temperature. After washes and brief incubation with DAPI, the slides were mounted in Elvanol and imaged. The following probes were used: ANXA1-c3 465411, LGR5-c2 311021, OLFM4-c1 311041, VIM-c1 310441. Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system using ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13).

It has been revealed that organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 h at room temperature, permeabilized in 0.6% Triton X-100 for 30 min, blocked with 5% BSA and 5% goat serum in PBS for 2 h, after which primary antibodies were added in blocking solution and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After multiple washes in PBS, secondary Alexa Fluor-conjugated antibodies were added in 1% BSA, 1% goat serum for 2 h at room temperature. Organoids were then mounted in ProLong Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486, 1:1,000, overnight, 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz, sc-101199, 1:500, overnight, 4 °C), active YAP (Abcam, ab205270, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977, 1:50, overnight, 4 °C), HP1α (Cell Signaling, 2616, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), lamin A/C (Cell Signaling, 2032, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), SOX4 (Abcam, ab236557, 1:400, overnight, 4 °C), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C). Images were obtained using either the Zeiss LSM980 or Nikon Yokogawa CSU-W1 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13) or NIS Elements (AR 5.41.01).

To mechanically compress the organoids, organoids grown in Matrigel for 5 days were replated on top of Matrigel-coated 12–20 mm round glass coverslips and allowed to attach for 24 h. After attachment, the organoids were sandwiched with another 12–20 mm coverslip with a weight applying 200 Pa of vertical stress (generating a 45% reduction in organoid height) for 20 h.

For 3D organoid imaging, single cells were first embedded in 8 mg ml−1 Matrigel and, after 4 days of culture, were transferred either to fresh Matrigel or pH-adjusted 1 mg ml−1 collagen I matrices. The organoids were treated with 5 µM TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042), 10 ng ml−1 TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) or both with daily medium replenishment while being live-cell imaged every 30 min with a Sartorius Incucyte S3 incubator microscope for up to 4 days.

It has been revealed that bright-field images were segmented using Cellpose4-SAM87 and edge detection followed by morphological gap-closing and hole-filling to obtain binary organoid masks that were imported to ImageJ (Fiji). MorphoLibJ88 was used to quantify convexity, Geodesic diameter, Geodesic elongation and organoid area that were scaled between 0 and 1 to initially classify the organoids into expanded, dispersive or cohesive classes in an unbiased manner. As the resolution of the masks was not sufficient to accurately capture surface structures, the classifications were all manually inspected further and assigned to the final classes.

Sources indicate that RNA was isolated using the NucleoSpin RNA plus Kit (Macherey-Nagel). RNA quality was assessed using the high-sensitivity RNA Screen Tape Analysis (TapeStation, Agilent) and subsequently 500 ng of RNA was reverse transcribed applying the SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was performed using the PowerUp SYBR Green Mastermix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on the QuantStudio5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gene expression was quantified using the ΔΔCt method with normalization to B2M. The following primers were used. B2M: forward primer, GAGTATGCCTGCCGTGTGAA; reverse primer, GCTTACATGTCTCGATCCCACT; AXIN2: forward primer, GCGCTGACGGATGATTCCAT; reverse primer, TGGGTTCTCGGGAAATGAGGT; ASCL2: forward primer, CGCCTACTCGTCGGACGACAG; reverse primer, GCCGCTCGCTCGGCTTCCG.

Industry observers note that mouse colonoscopy was performed using the TELE PACK+VET system (Karl Storz, RP101S1). Illumination was provided by a xenon light source connected through the Adapt. KST fibre-optic light cable/Xenon 100 (495KS). The system includes a camera control, air insufflation units and an integrated endoscopic video unit with built-in documentation and memory storage. Colonoscopy imaging was performed using an integrated multipurpose Hopkins Telescope (67031BA) with an outer diameter of 11.5 Fr. Images were acquired using an IMAGE1 S HX FULL HD Camera Head (TH110). Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and organoid fragments corresponding to 5 × 105 single cells were transplanted into the colonic submucosa using a Hamilton syringe (Hamilton, Reno, 7656-01) equipped with a transfer needle for sample loading (7770-02) and an injection needle (7803-05). The needle was carefully inserted into the colonic submucosa, and 50 µl of organoid fragments suspended in 1 mg ml−1 rat collagen type 1 (Sigma-Aldrich, C3867) supplemented with 10% Corning Matrigel (Corning, 356231) was delivered and generated a visible submucosal bleb. The mice were treated for 5 days after transplantation with the LATS kinase inhibitor TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042). TDI-011536 was prepared at a concentration of 5 mg ml−1 by emulsification in 10% Kolliphor HS 15 (Merck, 42966) in PBS and administered by oral gavage twice daily at a dose of 2.5 mg per kg. Vehicle-treated animals received 10% Kolliphor in PBS alone.

TGFβ1 treatment was performed using human recombinant TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) within Affi-Gel Blue beads (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 153-7301). In brief, beads were washed four times with ice-cold bi-distilled water and incubated overnight with 500 µl of 50 µg ml−1 TGFβ1 in PBS supplemented with 10 mM HEPES. TGFβ1-loaded beads were mixed with organoid fragments in collagen solution at a final proportion of 10% (v/v) before implantation. For dual-treatment experiments, animals received both TDI-011536 administration and TGFβ1-loaded beads as described above. Each treatment group consisted of four mice (n = 4). Mice were monitored three times per week, and colonoscopy imaging was performed every 2 weeks for 4 weeks before euthanasia.

According to recent reports, tissue biopsies (intestinal rolls) were fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin and sectioned. Sections were de-paraffinized using a graded alcohol series and antigen retrieval was carried out using target retrieval solution (Dako) at pH 6 or pH 9 in a pressure cooker. Unspecific binding was blocked using 5% normal goat serum, 3% BSA in PBS, after which antibodies were diluted in DAKO antibody diluent and incubated overnight in a moist chamber at 4 °C. After PBS washes, Alexa-Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies were diluted in 1% BSA in PBS, incubated for 1 h at room temperature, after which samples were mounted in Elvanol. The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108) and active YAP (Abcam ab205270). Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13). The tumour area was quantified using ANXA1 staining to generate a ROI mask in Fiji. The number of ROIs was used to extract the lesion number.

In a recent development, all animal experiments were performed in accordance with EU Directive 2010/63/EU and Finnish legislation, and were approved by the National Animal Experiment Board of Finland (ELLA) under project licence ESAVI/30305/2023. Female NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 005557) were used at 12 weeks of age at the start of the experiment. Sample size was determined using the resource equation method (E = N − T), where N is the total number of animals and T the number of groups; with four groups of four mice (N = 16), E = 12, within the recommended range of 10–20. Mice were randomly allocated to experimental groups; no formal randomization method was used. Tumour implantation was confirmed in all mice, and animals were euthanized and dissected 4 weeks after transplantation. No mice reached the humane end-point limits defined in the licence, and no mice were excluded from the analysis.

It has been revealed that statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad, v.9) or in R (v.2023.09.1+494). Statistical significance was determined using the specific tests indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Only two-tailed tests were used. In all cases in which a test for normally distributed data was used, normal distribution was confirmed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (α = 0.05). All experiments presented in the manuscript were repeated at least in three independent replicates. Automated software algorithms were used for unbiased quantification of staining intensities, sequencing data and architecture features/cell shapes in all experiments involving these techniques so blinding was not relevant. For animal experiments endoscopy and sample collection were performed in a blinded manner. For manual organoid invasion pattern classification blinding was applied during data analysis. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Sample size was determined based on previous experience, published literature, or to specific requirements of a given technique.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All patient-related data (TMA and spatial transcriptomics post-hoc staining) have been deposited in the Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193)89. All in vitro data are available from the authors on request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Venn diagrams summarizing the number of patients with quantified architecture in the tumour-core (CT) and invasive-margin (IM) compartments (bottom panel). Yellow dashed lines indicate the tumour–stroma boundary. Scale bar 200 µm. (d) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for patients stratified by nuclear circularity (high, medium, low) of tumour core (left) or invasive margin (right). P-values pairwise log-rank test. (h) Representative images of the six tumour architecture archetypes (scale bar 200 µm; architecture was quantified in 1,037 patients (a)).

Recent findings suggest that (a) Representative invasive margin sample with heterogeneous architectures (left panel), classifier predictions, projection of three closest neighbours’ distances, and relative alignment (order). Scale bar 400 µm. (b) t-SNE embedding of features derived from the U-Net from tiles used for classifier training. (c) Precision and recall of the tile classifier for architecture classification across classes, with error bars representing the standard deviation from five-fold cross-validation. (d) Schematic representation of quantified histological features, including neighbourhood, morphological and tumour-stroma interactions features. (e) Silhouette scores of the 196 manually selected archetype cores in morphological feature space (12 features from Fig. 1f: neighbourhood, stroma, morphology), compared to size-matched random draws from the MSS cohort with matching per-class label counts (n = 1,000 permutations). Distribution of mean silhouette scores across random draws (grey histogram) with the archetype value (black dashed line; left panel). Per-class silhouette (right panel): violins show the null distribution; diamonds mark the archetype silhouette for each architectural subtype. Archetypes form tighter, better-separated clusters than random draws overall and within each class, indicating that the manual curation captured genuine, well-defined exemplars of each architectural subtype rather than arbitrary selections.

According to recent reports, (a) Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models incorporating architecture types, with Glandular as the reference. Fragmented architecture remains significantly associated with poor survival after adjustment for other covariates. Estimated log hazard ratio (Cox regression coefficient) with 95% CI are shown; dashed vertical line at log(HR) = 0 indicates no effect (Wald tests with robust standard errors; p-values not adjusted for multiple comparisons). (b) Stacked bar plot displaying the distribution of architecture types across tumour stages, with left bars representing the tumour core and right bars representing the invasive margin. (c) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for stage II–III patients, stratified by architecture type from tumour core (CT) and invasive margin (IM). Patients with fragmented architectures exhibit poorer survival. (d) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for stage I–IV MSI patients, stratified by architecture type. (e, f) Kaplan-Meier survival curves of the validation dataset for MSS patients at stage I–IV (left) and stage II–III (right) (e) and for MSI patients at stage I–IV (f), stratified by architecture type. Validation dataset recapitulates poor survival in fragmented architecture MSS patients. (g) Sankey diagram illustrating the correspondence between CT and IM architecture classifications. (h) Distribution of the fragmentation index per TMA core, comparing values between the tumour core and invasive margin (paired sign-flip permutation test on log1p-transformed patient-level compartment means; n = 518 paired patients; boxplots show median IQR; 1.5×IQR whiskers). For all Kaplan-Meier curves p-values were from pairwise log-rank tests versus Glandular reference group.

(a) Stacked bar plot of budding grade distribution across architectures in tumour cores (CT). (b) Kaplan-Meier curves with low budding (BD1) grade, stratified by tumour architecture. (c) Distribution of intratumoral budding in CT classified as fragmented (left) or between mildly and strongly fragmented (right). (d, e) Normalized distribution of histological subtypes (d) and tumour grade (e; Low: grade 1–2; High: grade 3–4) across architecture types. Patients with unknown grade excluded. (f) Kaplan-Meier curves stratified by tumour architecture in CT (high-grade, left; low-grade, right; stages II–III; MSS; age <85). (g) Heatmap showing percentage of patients classified as fragmented within grade and tumour budding category (BD1: 0-4 buds; BD2: 5-9 buds; BD3: ≥10 buds; MSS; CT; age <85). (h) Hazard ratios (log scale) for disease-specific survival in stage II–III MSS (age <85). Patients with unknown budding or grade excluded. Analysis performed separately for CT (green) and IM (pink). Estimated log hazard ratio (Cox regression coefficient) with 95% CI; dashed vertical line at log(HR) = 0 indicates no effect, Wald tests with robust standard errors; p-values not adjusted for multiple comparisons). (i, j) Distribution of tumour location (i) and Immunoscore (j) across architecture classifications in MSS. Proportions normalized per architecture group. (k) Half-violin plots with embedded box plots showing per-core mean nuclear circularity (left) and solidity (right) for IM. Only IM cores with a dominant architecture (mixed cores excluded) and nuclear morphometry data were included; n is therefore lower than in Fig. 1h (871 IM patients). Each dot represents one TMA core; values are mean of all tumour nuclei within that core (n = 728 cores from 571 patients: Gland, n = 455 cores/372 patients; Sol, n = 24 cores/22 patients; Frag, n = 249 cores/206 patients; patient-level permutation tests on per-patient architecture means with Benjamini-Hochberg; boxplots show median, IQR; 1.5×IQR whiskers). For all Kaplan-Meier curves p-values were from pairwise log-rank tests versus Glandular group.

(a) Number of transcriptomic regions per patient, stratified by compartment (tumour core vs. invasive margin) and tissue type (tumour on left, stroma on right). (b) Distribution of molecular clusters across patients, demonstrating that each patient harbours unique clusters. (c) Distribution of architectural patterns among transcriptomic regions in each patient; most patients display heterogeneous architectures. (d) Distribution of molecular clusters across spatial clusters (excluding patients with few regions), where each spatial cluster is transcriptionally homogeneous. (e) Distribution of architecture types across spatial clusters (excluding patients with few regions), with each cluster exhibiting consistent architectural profiles. (f) Spatial projections of tumour slides for patients 6 (top) and 3 (bottom), with colour coding for architectures (left) and molecular clusters (right). Scale bar 5 mm. (g–i) Heatmaps showing the top 50 differentially expressed genes across architecture types for crypt base (g), regenerative stem cell (h), and EMT (i) gene sets.

Industry observers note that (a) Heatmap of key cell state and morphological marker levels in indicated cellular compartments across Leiden phenotypic cell macroclusters (cyto = cytoplasmic; nuc = nuclear). Grey bars indicate cell number in each cluster. Diff = differentiated, Reg = regenerative. (b) Bar graph of distribution of cell macroclusters to generate patient-scale phenotypic groups. Grey bars indicate the number of patients in each group. (c) Representative immunofluorescence images (out of 1037 patients) of ANXA1, TNC, CDX2, pan-cytokeratin (panCK), and Ki67 stainings of patient TMAs in the main phenotypic groups to identify relationships of cell phenotypes with tumour architecture. Numbers indicate the corresponding zoomed regions (white rectangles in upper panel). Colours indicate the corresponding molecular clusters. Scale bars 200 µm (upper panel), 100 µm (lower panel).

(a) Representative images of TMA cores illustrating four architecture-epithelial state combinations (1: Gland-Reg/EMT; 2: Gland-Prox1; 3: Frag-Proliferative; 4: Frag-Diff). Top row: composite immunofluorescence overlay (DAPI, ANXA1, PROX1, CDX2, panCK, Ki67). Middle rows: individual channel images for each marker (DAPI, ANXA1, TNC, PROX1, VIM, CDX2, panCK, Ki67, E-Cadherin). Bottom row: cell-level epithelial state classification maps with per-cell colour coding (PROX1, (Diff-Low, Diff-High, Diff-Mid, Proliferative, Reg/EMT, EMT VIM; scale bars 200 µm; 100 µm)). (b) Kaplan-Meier curve of disease-specific survival across architecture and tumour phenotypic composite groups in invasive margin (IM; pairwise log-rank tests versus the Gland-Diff High reference group). (c) Kaplan-Meier curves for disease-specific survival in stage II-III patients, stratified by combined architecture–epithelial state categories in tumour core (CT; top) and IM (bottom). Fragmented-Regen/EMT tumours show the worst prognosis in the CT (pairwise log-rank tests versus the Gland-Diff-High reference group). (d) Kaplan-Meier curves for disease-specific survival stratified by dominant tumour epithelial state in the core tumour (CT, top) and invasive margin (IM, bottom). No significant survival differences were observed between epithelial states in the CT. In contrast, Diff-Low and Regen/EMT states associate with worse prognosis in the IM (pairwise log-rank tests versus the Diff-High reference group). (e) Sankey diagram plot showing the redistribution of architecture–epithelial state combinations between CT and IM compartments. Most patients with fragmented regenerative tumour cores also showed the same signature at the invasive margin, whereas the reverse pattern was less frequent. Gland = glandular, Frag = fragmented, Reg = regenerative, Diff = differentiated.

It has been revealed that (a) Quantification of SNAIL1, VIM, and nuclear/cytoplasmic ANXA1 immunofluorescence across three tumour architectures, derived from multiple regions of two whole-slide sections from two patients (two-sided Mann-Whitney/Benjamini-Hochberg (BH)). (b) Projected mean intensity of nuclear and cytoplasmic ANXA1 in individual tumour cells at the invasive front of Patient 8 exhibiting moderate fragmentation (top panels), corresponding box-and-violin plots (lower panel) show ANXA1 intensity across distance bins relative to the invasive front. Cell intensities were averaged within 100 × 100 µm spatial blocks, and adjacent distance bins were compared (two-sided Mann-Whitney; Benjamini-Hochberg (BH); scale bar 200 µm). (c) Representative images of E-cadherin and SNAIL1-stained glandular, moderately/highly fragmented regions. Scale bar 100 µm. (d) Projected mean spatial-coherence score calculated for each tile, grouped by (i) homotypic and (ii) heterotypic cell pairs. Positive scores reflect stronger-than-random co-localization, whereas negative scores indicate spatial avoidance. Dot size scales with relative abundance of cell types. Box plot highlights spatial-coherence of each tile across different pairs (n = 138 tiles from one patient; 41,477 tumour cells: 21,463 VIM-high and 20,014 ANXA1-high; paired Wilcoxon/BH). (e) Changes in spatial clusters (top) and architecture types (bottom) along pseudotime, profiled within consecutive sliding windows. (f) Tile-level U-Net embedding features projected into two dimensions and coloured by predicted architecture class. The overlaid PAGA trajectory depicts the inferred path through embedding space from glandular-like tiles toward fragmented/solid architectures (left). Architecture probabilities averaged across pseudotime bins along this trajectory (middle). Cell phenotype fractions were mapped onto the same pseudotime axis (right). All boxplots show median, IQR, 1.5×IQR whiskers.

(a) Boxplot (median, IQR, 1.5×IQR whiskers) representing nuclear shape descriptors (circularity and solidity) averaged per transcriptomic region for 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. Each dot represents one AOI (linear mixed-effects model with patient as a random intercept, contrasting fragmented architectures “fragmented and moderately fragmented” pooled against “solid, glandular dense, glandular, and glandular infiltrated” pooled classes; two-sided permutation tests stratified by patient to account for repeated tumour AOIs within patients, n.s. = not significant). (b) Dot plot of immune and stromal cell-type signature enrichment in GeoMx stroma AOIs across tumour architectures (n = 76 stroma AOIs from 6 patients). Each dot represents a cell-type gene signature (columns) within a given architecture (rows). Dot colour indicates the mean z-scored module score across AOIs, with red and blue denoting relative enrichment and depletion, respectively. Dot size reflects the percentage of AOIs with a z-score exceeding 0.5. Z-scores were computed across all stroma AOIs irrespective of architecture.

(a) UMAP of Leiden clusters from sc-RNAseq data of patient-derived organoids (line 2) treated with TDI-011536 (YAPa), TGF-β1 or both.
